title: AI Workflow challenges
author: FondantIcy866
selftext:
I have no gamedev or coding experience. The thing that has been really hard for me is the proliferation of documents claude makes, and how hard it is to keep track. I asked it to research game dev industry best practices, so it came up with a system. It makes and maintains a roadmap and documents for each system's design, specs, "calls", "ideas", and some other things. And then a ton of other stuff has been generated.

The problem is that it makes stuff that I never see unless I closely read every document (which I don't), and then it later it refers to that stuff it made as if it were my "calls" and treats it like the word of god.

I do not want to actually have to read all this stuff, but telling it to record less information risks losing important stuff I don't want to lose. 

Most of what I've been doing is building a functioning economy for my game. Which involves trying lots of formulas and parameters on paper. It constantly takes a parameter (e.g. "food should cost 2x what wood costs") which is a value we use in one experiment, and then treats it as a holy grail forever and I don't realize it unless I constantly re-scrutinize everything.

That's just one example I've been dealing with a lot.

Anyways, I'd love advice of how to deal with this.

Thanks!

comments.author: Similar_Guide4193
comments.body:
I turned off memories, it was like a second set of instructions that was often just contradictory to my documentation.

And I put in [Claude.MD](http://Claude.MD) to not record anything as documentation unless specifically requested. Optionally add to ask you if it thinks it should be.

\[edit\] To fix your current issue, ask it todo a full review to cut documentation that isn't neccessary and work with the AI on this for an hour or two (by asking questions etc) before commiting to cut the documentation.

comments.body: This post reminds me one project manager I once worked with who don't know how to program at all. That several months was a very painful experience to me...

How do you know?

Jokes aside, you need to learn some game design or coding if you want to be able to understand what's being saved. Otherwise if you're just vibecoding, then accept that there is documentation you aren't in a position to assess anyway.

replies.body: Yes I am vibecoding, and I am not assessing it all. I accept. But curious if people have suggestions for workflow and managing all the documentation that is more effective. Thanks.

comments.author: Previous-Tackle-759
comments.body:
Small disclaimer first: I've been in IT for 25 years, so I know what all this documentation is for and reading it doesn't hurt me the way it hurts you. Maybe that makes my advice a bit unfair for your situation. But I had exactly the same "Claude treats its own notes as my decisions" problem, and this is what fixed it:

* **Every record gets a status: decision, hypothesis, or superseded.** And one rule in CLAUDE.md: "Only I make decisions. Anything you propose or test is a hypothesis until I say yes." Your "food costs 2x wood" would have stayed a hypothesis with a date on it.
* **One fact, one place.** Decisions live in one file, one line each. Everything else (specs, reviews, hand-overs) can only point to it, never restate it. Then you only need to read that one file.
* **Numbers live in a data file, not in prose.** Docs say "food is more expensive than wood", the actual number sits in one config. Changing the experiment means changing one value.
* **Compress regularly.** Once in a while ask Claude to move everything superseded into an archive folder and keep only what's current. Nothing gets lost, it just stops shouting.

You don't need to read 480 pages. You need one page that you actually agree with.

replies.author: FondantIcy866
replies.body:
Super helpful, thank you!

For the first one: if I propose a value for the purposes of moving forward (e.g. "let's try food = 2 x wood"), that's still a hypothesis, even though I said it. Whereas I have ID'd some things as definite targets that are more or less settled (e.g. max walking speed, because anything faster would look crazy). Does that make sense? Kind of makes me want a me-hypothesis and claude-hypothesis option.

replies.author: Previous-Tackle-759
replies.body:
Yes, exactly - status is about how settled it is, not who said it. I'd keep "who" as a separate field (source: me / claude) rather than splitting the status. The useful rule then is one line: only you can move something to "decision". Claude can propose hypotheses all day, but never promotes its own.

And give each hypothesis a way to check it. Something like "food = 2x wood" is an economy number, so it's checked with a small simulation first: how many minutes of play until the player can afford X, where resources pile up, what runs dry. Claude writes that script easily. After launch, analytics confirms or kills it: log what players actually gather and spend, and compare with the model. Otherwise the number just sits there long enough to look like a fact.

replies.author: FondantIcy866
replies.body: Makes sense, thank you. And when you say numbers in a data file you mean json or something, not the normal markdowns?

replies.author: Previous-Tackle-759
replies.body: >Yes - anything code can read, JSON is totally fine. The rule is markdown says why, data says how much, so a number lives in one place and docs only point to it. In my case the game reads its own data files, and everything gets indexed into SQLite, so agents query numbers instead of reading through docs. But that's habit, any format works as long as there's one source.
